standard.title: Language, setting and mood
standard.description: discuss how an author uses language and illustrations to portray characters and settings and create mood
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how language presents characters and settings differently across texts (AC9E2LE03). They have not yet examined how language and illustrations together create mood — the atmosphere or feeling a text establishes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss how authors use language and illustrations to portray characters and settings and create mood.

nodes.label: Language portrayals of character and setting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify descriptive language that creates character and setting, and discuss what the language choices reveal about traits, relationships and place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two descriptive language choices that portray a character or setting, and explain what each reveals.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss how descriptive language creates setting, how it portrays character traits and actions, and how characters' speech and actions reveal personality — connecting language choices to their effect on the reader.
wider: Compare how the same character is described at different points in the story and discuss how the language changes as the character changes
Find language choices that portray setting in a First Nations Australian text and discuss how the relationship with Country/Place is constructed through language differently from other settings
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify and interpret descriptive language choices at N1 lack the analytical vocabulary needed to discuss how language and illustration work together to create mood at N2.

response_modes.reason: Students need to encounter descriptive language choices across multiple text types — narrative, picture books, poetry — before the concept of language as a deliberate constructive choice becomes stable. A single exemplar risks anchoring the concept too narrowly.

success_criteria: Student identifies specific language choices (not just general description) that portray a character or setting
Student discusses what the language reveals — trait, relationship, place quality — not just what it describes

nodes.label: Creating mood through language and illustration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify mood in a text and discuss how specific language choices and illustrations work together to create it.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the mood of a text or a section and explain at least one language or illustration choice that creates that mood.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how descriptive language creates setting and influences mood; identify how illustrations portray mood alongside or beyond what the words say; discuss how language and illustration work together to create atmosphere.
wider: Compare the mood created at different points in the same story and discuss how the author shifts mood through language and illustration choices
Find a text where the illustration creates a different or ironic mood from the written language, and discuss the effect of that contrast

response_modes.reason: Students often identify mood as a feeling the character has, rather than an atmosphere the whole text creates for the reader. Multiple examples — across different genres, with and without illustrations — help students distinguish between character emotion and textual mood.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Mood analysis through combined language and illustration is rich and directly accessible for Y3 through picture books and illustrated texts. The interplay of verbal and visual mood-making is a genuine conceptual extension — understanding that mood can be created through both modes simultaneously.
success_criteria: Student names the mood created in a text (not just the character's emotion)
Student identifies at least one specific language or illustration choice that creates that mood and explains how
